claims.claim: The corresponding fitness costs of resistance mutations range from almost none to a 25% reduction of the population growth rate.
claims.source: The corresponding fitness costs range from almost none to a 25% reduction of the population growth rate and show a very weak positive correlation (R2 = 0.07, p=0.09) with (log) benefit over all studies taken together (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Fitness costs of resistance mutations show a very weak positive correlation (R2 = 0.07, p=0.09) with (log) benefit over all studies taken together.
claims.source: The corresponding fitness costs range from almost none to a 25% reduction of the population growth rate and show a very weak positive correlation (R2 = 0.07, p=0.09) with (log) benefit over all studies taken together (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis of the compiled data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Mutations seem likely to incur more costs than benefits.
claims.source: In general, mutations seem likely to incur more costs than benefits.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the data shown in Figure 1B and the literature review.

claims.claim: The average benefit of resistance mutations to AMPs is substantially lower than for commonly used ABs.
claims.source: Notably, our literature search suggests a difference in mutational benefit available for two different antimicrobials: the average benefit of resistance mutations to AMPs is substantially lower than for commonly used ABs (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data compiled in Table 1 and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The probability of treatment failure was always close to 1 for single-step resistance evolution.
claims.source: We found that the probability of treatment failure was always close to 1 for single-step resistance evolution, but decreased rapidly if multiple mutations were required.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The probability of treatment failure decreased rapidly if multiple mutations were required.
claims.source: We found that the probability of treatment failure was always close to 1 for single-step resistance evolution, but decreased rapidly if multiple mutations were required.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: If three mutations were necessary to overcome the applied dose, the probability of pathogen survival approached 0.
claims.source: Notably, already if three mutations were necessary to overcome the applied dose, the probability of pathogen survival approached 0 (Figure 2A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The qualitative picture of the results was not dependent on the specific cost-benefit correlation assumed for most simulations.
claims.source: The qualitative picture of these results was not dependent on the specific cost-benefit correlation that we are assuming for most of our simulations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the robustness analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Higher genetic diversity increases the probability that some individuals will be able to survive a given environment.
claims.source: One aspect of resistance evolution that is especially important when considering multiple mutations is the mutational diversity that arises in the pathogen population: high genetic diversity (here meaning diversity in the resistance phenotype) increases the probability that some individuals will be able to survive a given environment – such as treatment with other drugs (Castro et al., 2020) – and increases the adaptive potential overall (Van Egeren et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Castro et al., 2020 and Van Egeren et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Higher mutational diversity was observed with single-step than multi-step resistance evolution.
claims.source: Using the Shannon index to determine the highest mutational diversity obtained in the population over the treatment period, we clearly observed higher diversity with single-step than multi-step resistance evolution (Figure 2B), even if we increased the mutation rate proportionally to the number of mutations required (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: A mutant strain can invade at the mutant-free equilibrium if the death rate of the sensitive strain is higher than the death rate of the mutant.
claims.source: It can be shown analytically that a mutant strain can invade at the mutant-free equilibrium if the death rate of the sensitive strain is higher than the death rate of the mutant, where the mutant death rate is a combination of intrinsic and drug-induced death as well as the mutational cost (Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is an analytical result derived from the model equations presented in the Materials and methods section.

claims.claim: At high drug doses and low benefits, reduced diversity is due to extinction.
claims.source: The observed higher diversity with single-step patterns seems counterintuitive as the need for multiple mutations should increase diversity (Figure 2B), but can be explained as follows: at high drug doses and low benefits, this effect is due to extinction that effectively reduces genetic diversity, while at low doses and high benefits, high mutational costs inhibit the build-up of diversity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: At low doses and high benefits, high mutational costs inhibit the build-up of diversity.
claims.source: The observed higher diversity with single-step patterns seems counterintuitive as the need for multiple mutations should increase diversity (Figure 2B), but can be explained as follows: at high drug doses and low benefits, this effect is due to extinction that effectively reduces genetic diversity, while at low doses and high benefits, high mutational costs inhibit the build-up of diversity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Resistance alleles with low costs are favored.
claims.source: These findings agree with an experimental study showing that resistance alleles with low costs are favored (Wichelhaus et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wichelhaus et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Constant PKs distinctly lowered the probability of treatment failure and the emergence of mutational diversity.
claims.source: Whereas constant PKs distinctly lowered the probability of treatment failure and the emergence of mutational diversity, peak and ramp PKs showed similar magnitudes of resistance evolution (Figure 3B, C, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3B, C and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Peak and ramp PKs showed similar magnitudes of resistance evolution.
claims.source: Whereas constant PKs distinctly lowered the probability of treatment failure and the emergence of mutational diversity, peak and ramp PKs showed similar magnitudes of resistance evolution (Figure 3B, C, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3B, C and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Ramp PKs lead to more than twice the mutational diversity with multi-step resistance patterns compared to peak PKs.
claims.source: However, ramp PKs lead to more than twice the mutational diversity with multi-step resistance patterns (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), which suggests that treatment failure and pathogen diversity are connected in a non-trivial manner: while higher mutational diversity increases the risk of resistance evolution, neither its presence nor absence is obviously predictive of the treatment outcome (Figure 2, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Treatment failure and pathogen diversity are connected in a non-trivial manner.
claims.source: However, ramp PKs lead to more than twice the mutational diversity with multi-step resistance patterns (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), which suggests that treatment failure and pathogen diversity are connected in a non-trivial manner: while higher mutational diversity increases the risk of resistance evolution, neither its presence nor absence is obviously predictive of the treatment outcome (Figure 2, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results comparing diversity and treatment failure across different conditions.

claims.claim: AMP treatments are characterized by higher killing rates, steeper dose-response curves, and lower mutation rates than AB treatments.
claims.source: Briefly, AMP treatments are characterized by higher killing rates, steeper dose-response curves (Figure 1A), and lower mutation rates than AB ones (Yu et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2018 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Treatment failure and mutational diversity was lower for AMPs with peak and constant PK treatments.
claims.source: Consistent with previous findings that AMPs lead to a lower risk of resistance evolution and a narrower mutant selection window (MSW) than ABs (Yu et al., 2018), treatment failure and mutational diversity was lower for AMPs with peak and constant PK treatments (Figures 2 and 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figures 2 and 3, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Mutations accumulate at sublethal drug doses.
claims.source: Notably, in accordance with empirical studies (Andersson and Hughes, 2014), we generally see mutations accumulating at sublethal drug doses, but the maximal diversity is substantially lower in AMP treatments (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2B and a citation to Andersson and Hughes, 2014.

claims.claim: The maximal diversity is substantially lower in AMP treatments compared to AB treatments.
claims.source: Notably, in accordance with empirical studies (Andersson and Hughes, 2014), we generally see mutations accumulating at sublethal drug doses, but the maximal diversity is substantially lower in AMP treatments (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The steeper dose-response curve of AMPs makes their resistance dynamics more sensitive to the shape of the PK than those of ABs.
claims.source: Interestingly, the steeper dose-response curve of AMPs seems to make their resistance dynamics more sensitive to the shape of the PK than those of ABs (Figures 2 and 3, Figure 3—figure supplements 1, 2, and 4): in contrast to the other two PK profiles, ramp PKs lead to a drastic increase in treatment failure with AMPs, especially in multi-step scenarios (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results shown in Figures 2 and 3 and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Ramp PKs lead to a drastic increase in treatment failure with AMPs, especially in multi-step scenarios.
claims.source: Interestingly, the steeper dose-response curve of AMPs seems to make their resistance dynamics more sensitive to the shape of the PK than those of ABs (Figures 2 and 3, Figure 3—figure supplements 1, 2, and 4): in contrast to the other two PK profiles, ramp PKs lead to a drastic increase in treatment failure with AMPs, especially in multi-step scenarios (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: For ramp PKs, AMPs did not perform better and under some conditions even worse than ABs.
claims.source: Accordingly, for ramp PKs, AMPs did not perform better and under some conditions even worse than ABs (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: There is an intermediate range of ramp duration (48–84 hr) which showed increased treatment failure with AMPs over ABs.
claims.source: By varying the ramp duration (or equivalently the rate of drug uptake), we found that there is an intermediate range (48–84 hr), which showed increased treatment failure with AMPs over ABs (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A.

claims.claim: A narrow MSW can lead to optimal selection conditions for the sequential emergence of increasingly higher resistance mutations with ramp PKs.
claims.source: Paradoxically, while a narrow MSW generally hinders the emergence of numerous mutations in the population, for ramp PKs it can lead to optimal selection conditions for the sequential emergence of increasingly higher resistance mutations due to the strong selection for the next mutation combined with sufficient time for its emergence.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results and analysis of selection coefficients shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5B.

claims.claim: The risk of multi-step resistance is increased if AMPs are used with ramp treatments as compared to the other PKs.
claims.source: Hence, especially the risk of multi-step resistance is increased if AMPs are used with ramp treatments as compared to the other PKs (Figure 3B, C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3B, C.

claims.claim: The number of resistance mutations was the main determinant of treatment outcome.
claims.source: Overall, the number of resistance mutations was the main determinant of treatment outcome, but we also found a complex dependence on PK and PD characteristics.
claims.evidence: This is a summary inference from all the simulation results presented in the paper.

claims.claim: Bacteriostatic antimicrobials slow down the rise of mutations in comparison to bactericidal ones only for ramp and constant PK treatments.
claims.source: We would expect bacteriostatic antimicrobials to slow down the rise of mutations in comparison to bactericidal ones as the acquisition of mutations is also coupled to bacterial growth. However, we find that this is only true for ramp and constant PK treatments (Figure 3—figure supplement 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6A.

claims.claim: Peak PKs allow for regrowth of bacterial cells due to drug decay, which increases bacterial survival and treatment failure, especially with multi-step resistance.
claims.source: Peak PKs allow for regrowth of bacterial cells due to drug decay, which increases bacterial survival and treatment failure, especially with multi-step resistance.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results comparing bacteriostatic and bactericidal drug action.

claims.claim: Mutational diversity only increased for AMP treatments when considering bacteriostatic action.
claims.source: Interestingly, mutational diversity only increased for AMP treatments (Figure 3—figure supplement 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6B.

claims.claim: Adaptive treatment is called adaptive because drug doses are adapted to keep the sensitive population as big as possible and the total pathogen burden below a given limit.
claims.source: This strategy is called adaptive treatment as drug doses are adapted to keep the sensitive population as big as possible and the total pathogen burden below a given limit.
claims.evidence: This is a definition of adaptive treatment.

claims.claim: In adaptive treatment, the sensitive population provides a benefit by competitively inhibiting the resistant subpopulation, but also a risk by supplying mutational input.
claims.source: In adaptive treatment, the sensitive population provides a benefit by competitively inhibiting the resistant subpopulation, but also a risk by supplying mutational input (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is a conceptual explanation of the trade-off in adaptive treatment, illustrated in Figure 4.

claims.claim: There is a threshold for the size of the pre-existent resistant subpopulation above which adaptive treatment is more effective than aggressive 'eradication' in containing the infection.
claims.source: This trade-off creates a threshold for the size of the pre-existent resistant subpopulation above which adaptive treatment is more effective than aggressive 'eradication' in containing the infection (Hansen et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hansen et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The resistant subpopulation threshold above which adaptive treatment is more beneficial can be much lower in the multi-step scenario than in the single-step one.
claims.source: When we incorporated adaptive treatment in our multi-step resistance framework (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), we found that the resistant subpopulation threshold above which adaptive treatment is more beneficial can be much lower in the multi-step scenario than in the single-step one (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analytical and simulation results shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: With multi-step resistance there is a smaller population to supply resistant bacteria than with single-step resistance.
claims.source: This can be intuitively explained by the fact that all (partially) sensitive bacteria serve as competitors for fully resistant cells, but only the subpopulation one mutation away from being fully resistant constitutes the risk population (Figure 4B). Thus, with multi-step resistance there is a smaller population to supply resistant bacteria than with single-step resistance, changing the trade-off towards adaptive treatment.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the model structure illustrated in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The difference between adaptive and aggressive treatment in the duration until treatment failure can be several-fold larger for multi-step than single-step resistance patterns.
claims.source: Additionally (in scenarios where adaptive treatment is favorable), the difference between adaptive and aggressive treatment in the duration until treatment failure can be several-fold larger for multi-step than single-step resistance patterns (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Assuming either single- or multi-step evolution could lead to considerably different treatment strategy assessments with regard to treatment failure through resistant pathogens.
claims.source: Hence, assuming either single- or multi-step evolution could lead to considerably different treatment strategy assessments with regard to treatment failure through resistant pathogens.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the results on adaptive treatment shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: HGT carriers dominated the remaining pathogen population at the end of the treatment.
claims.source: Even though HGT carriers dominated the remaining pathogen population at the end of the treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), the addition of HGT did not change the probability of treatment failure (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The addition of HGT did not change the probability of treatment failure.
claims.source: Even though HGT carriers dominated the remaining pathogen population at the end of the treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), the addition of HGT did not change the probability of treatment failure (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Initial rescue of the population is due to mutations, whereas HGT resistance is acquired later during the infection.
claims.source: Consequently, initial rescue of the population is due to mutations – and therefore dependent on the magnitude of the mutational benefit – whereas HGT resistance is acquired later during the infection, after which it spreads rapidly.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results with HGT.

claims.claim: Drug resistance requiring more than one mutation will arise more slowly.
claims.source: While it is intuitive that drug resistance requiring more than one mutation will arise more slowly, we find that it can be a surprisingly strong inhibitor of resistance evolution and mutational diversity, depending on the drug class and administration route (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a general inference supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Multi-step resistance can be a surprisingly strong inhibitor of resistance evolution and mutational diversity, depending on the drug class and administration route.
claims.source: While it is intuitive that drug resistance requiring more than one mutation will arise more slowly, we find that it can be a surprisingly strong inhibitor of resistance evolution and mutational diversity, depending on the drug class and administration route (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The number of mutations necessary for resistance strongly affects predictions of treatment outcome and optimality with regard to antimicrobial resistance.
claims.source: We demonstrated that the number of mutations necessary for resistance strongly affects predictions of treatment outcome and optimality with regard to antimicrobial resistance – in a manner that is robust to variations in mutation rates and in the cost per mutation (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results and robustness analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 5.

claims.claim: Mutational input limited to low benefits leads to decreased drug resistance evolution as compared to systems in which high-benefit mutations are available.
claims.source: Experimental support for our simulation results comes from studies reporting that mutational input limited to low benefits (Drlica, 2003) leads to decreased drug resistance evolution as compared to systems, in which high-benefit mutations are available (Allen et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Drlica, 2003 and Allen et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Limited access to high-benefit mutations seems to curtail MIC increase beyond a certain threshold.
claims.source: Moreover, limited access to high-benefit mutations seems to curtail MIC increase beyond a certain threshold (Chevereau et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chevereau et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The magnitude of the resistance benefit correlates with the mechanism of resistance.
claims.source: The pattern of resistance evolution (single- and multi-step) is likely to be associated with the molecular mechanisms of resistance for a given antimicrobial: as an overall rule, the magnitude of the resistance benefit correlates with the mechanism of resistance, for example, efflux pumps yield low benefits, whereas specific drug target mutations yield high benefits (Hughes and Andersson, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hughes and Andersson, 2017.

claims.claim: Efflux pumps yield low resistance benefits.
claims.source: The pattern of resistance evolution (single- and multi-step) is likely to be associated with the molecular mechanisms of resistance for a given antimicrobial: as an overall rule, the magnitude of the resistance benefit correlates with the mechanism of resistance, for example, efflux pumps yield low benefits, whereas specific drug target mutations yield high benefits (Hughes and Andersson, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hughes and Andersson, 2017.

claims.claim: Specific drug target mutations yield high resistance benefits.
claims.source: The pattern of resistance evolution (single- and multi-step) is likely to be associated with the molecular mechanisms of resistance for a given antimicrobial: as an overall rule, the magnitude of the resistance benefit correlates with the mechanism of resistance, for example, efflux pumps yield low benefits, whereas specific drug target mutations yield high benefits (Hughes and Andersson, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hughes and Andersson, 2017.

claims.claim: MIC increase was low for drugs which typically show unspecific resistance mechanisms via two-component systems or lipopolysaccharide modifications.
claims.source: Overall, however, MIC increase was low for drugs, which typically show unspecific resistance mechanisms via two-component systems or lipopolysaccharide modifications – as generally seen for AMP resistance (Lofton et al., 2013; Makarova et al., 2018; Kubicek-Sutherland et al., 2017) – and high for drugs with typical resistance via specific target modifications, as seen for some AB classes (e.g., rifampicin resistance via RNAP subunit mutations) (Goldstein, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: MIC increase was high for drugs with typical resistance via specific target modifications.
claims.source: Overall, however, MIC increase was low for drugs, which typically show unspecific resistance mechanisms via two-component systems or lipopolysaccharide modifications – as generally seen for AMP resistance (Lofton et al., 2013; Makarova et al., 2018; Kubicek-Sutherland et al., 2017) – and high for drugs with typical resistance via specific target modifications, as seen for some AB classes (e.g., rifampicin resistance via RNAP subunit mutations) (Goldstein, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Goldstein, 2014.

claims.claim: Resistance evolution in biofilms is prone to occur through unspecific mechanisms, even if specific mechanisms are favored in planktonic cultures.
claims.source: A recent study also suggests that resistance evolution in biofilms, which are often associated with clinical infections, is prone to occur through unspecific mechanisms, even if specific mechanisms are favored in planktonic cultures (Santos-Lopez et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Santos-Lopez et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The risk of resistance evolution does not seem to be related to the emerging mutational diversity in the population in a trivial manner.
claims.source: Interestingly, the risk of resistance evolution does not seem to be related to the emerging mutational diversity in the population in a trivial manner as it is either limited by fast extinction or high mutational cost (Figure 2, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claims.claim: Mutational diversity can increase adaptation by fixing more mildly deleterious mutations, which can then act as stepping stones for multi-drug resistance evolution.
claims.source: Reducing mutational diversity is however a worthwhile goal in its own right as mutational diversity can increase adaptation by fixing more mildly deleterious mutations, which can then act as stepping stones for multi-drug resistance evolution (Van Egeren et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Van Egeren et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The diversity arising during the treatment period will help to determine if escalating the drug dose is expected to be beneficial.
claims.source: Further, the diversity arising during the treatment period will help to determine if escalating the drug dose is expected to be beneficial or if, conversely, it would be detrimental because higher-resistance mutations are already present in the population and would be selected.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the clinical implications of mutational diversity.

claims.claim: The number of resistance mutations emerging over the treatment can be useful in estimating the width of the MSW.
claims.source: Hence, the number of resistance mutations emerging over the treatment can be useful in estimating the width of the MSW – even though the diversity remaining at the end of the treatment will likely be lower (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is an inference supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Mutational diversity arises from a combination of selection pressure, bacterial growth, and fitness costs.
claims.source: We find that mutational diversity arises from a combination of selection pressure, bacterial growth, and fitness costs and cannot be predicted from the mutational benefit or the probability of treatment failure alone.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results across different conditions.

claims.claim: Drug choice should be dependent not only on the PD characteristics, but also the specific drug PK in the target body compartment.
claims.source: Diversity is also shaped in unexpected ways by interactions between the drug type and drug concentration changes, making drug choice not only dependent on the PD characteristics, but also the specific drug PK in the target body compartment.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results showing complex interactions between PK and PD.

claims.claim: Purely bacteriostatic effects can lead to different trends for PK and PD influence on treatment failure and mutational diversity, making peak PKs the least favorable drug administration route.
claims.source: While we mostly focused on the action of bactericidal drugs in this study, we note that purely bacteriostatic effects can lead to different trends for PK and PD influence on treatment failure and mutational diversity, for example, making peak PKs the least favorable drug administration route (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claims.claim: κ governs not only the size of the MSW, but generally shapes the selection pressure for resistance evolution in a qualitative manner.
claims.source: By analyzing the selection coefficients for various treatments, we find that κ governs not only the size of the MSW (Yu et al., 2018; Chevereau et al., 2015), but generally shapes the selection pressure for resistance evolution in a qualitative manner.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the selection coefficient analysis, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Natural AMP expression patterns in the producing organisms resemble ramp PKs.
claims.source: This is noteworthy as natural AMP expression patterns in the producing organisms resemble ramp PKs (Johnston et al., 2014; Haine et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Johnston et al., 2014 and Haine et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Natural AMP production in cocktails is favorable because AMP cocktails will limit the selection pressure and potential for resistance evolution to individual components.
claims.source: This finding could suggest another reason why natural AMP production in cocktails is favorable (Zanchi et al., 2017) as AMP cocktails will limit the selection pressure and potential for resistance evolution to individual components.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference from the simulation results, supported by a citation to Zanchi et al., 2017.

claims.claim: A high probability of treatment failure is still mostly observed with high mutational benefits.
claims.source: However, a high probability of treatment failure is still mostly observed with high mutational benefits (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), that is, limited with the small-benefit mutations likely associated with multi-step resistance (Jochumsen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Jochumsen et al., 2016.

claims.claim: AMP-like colistin and daptomycin are typically applied as (short) IV treatments.
claims.source: AMP-like colistin and daptomycin, for example, are typically applied as (short) IV treatments (Liu et al., 2011; Tsuji et al., 2019), which resemble peak PKs, and they are still active as last-resort drugs for multi-drug-resistant bacterial pathogens (Liu et al., 2011; Tsuji et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2011 and Tsuji et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Colistin and daptomycin are still active as last-resort drugs for multi-drug-resistant bacterial pathogens.
claims.source: AMP-like colistin and daptomycin, for example, are typically applied as (short) IV treatments (Liu et al., 2011; Tsuji et al., 2019), which resemble peak PKs, and they are still active as last-resort drugs for multi-drug-resistant bacterial pathogens (Liu et al., 2011; Tsuji et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2011 and Tsuji et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Multi-step patterns seem to be the common mechanism by which AMP resistance evolves.
claims.source: This is particularly notable as multi-step patterns seem to be the common mechanism by which AMP resistance evolves (Table 1; Spohn et al., 2019; Jochumsen et al., 2016; Joo et al., 2016) – thereby suggesting another advantage over ABs, for which single- and multi-step evolution is common (Drlica, 2003; Weinreich et al., 2006; Wistrand-Yuen et al., 2018; Marcusson et al., 2009; Jin and Gross, 1988).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the data in Table 1 and citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: For ABs, single- and multi-step evolution is common.
claims.source: This is particularly notable as multi-step patterns seem to be the common mechanism by which AMP resistance evolves (Table 1; Spohn et al., 2019; Jochumsen et al., 2016; Joo et al., 2016) – thereby suggesting another advantage over ABs, for which single- and multi-step evolution is common (Drlica, 2003; Weinreich et al., 2006; Wistrand-Yuen et al., 2018; Marcusson et al., 2009; Jin and Gross, 1988).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: Distributions of mutational effects have rarely been characterized experimentally for drug resistance.
claims.source: Unfortunately, distributions of mutational effects have rarely been characterized experimentally for drug resistance, and even then only for a single mutational step (Chevereau et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the state of experimental data, supported by a citation to Chevereau et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Information about distributions of mutational effects is crucial as input for PKPD models to accurately predict resistance evolution and population diversity in response to drug treatment.
claims.source: We show, however, that this information is crucial as input for PKPD models to accurately predict resistance evolution and population diversity in response to drug treatment.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results showing the importance of mutational benefit and cost parameters.

claims.claim: Benefit and costs of individual mutations involved in multi-step resistance to a single drug are likely to vary.
claims.source: Even between mutations involved in multi-step resistance to a single drug, benefit and costs of individual mutations are likely to vary (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Epistasis in benefit and or cost magnitude can facilitate or preclude certain evolutionary pathways.
claims.source: In addition, epistasis in benefit and or cost magnitude can facilitate or preclude certain evolutionary pathways (Jochumsen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jochumsen et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The main results with regard to PD and PK influence on single- and multi-step resistance are expected to be robust to changes in epistasis.
claims.source: Both options can be easily included in our model, but empirical data in this regard is sparse, and we expect our main results with regard to PD and PK influence on single- and multi-step resistance to be robust to such changes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the robustness of the results.

claims.claim: Compensatory mutations can influence the dynamics of resistance evolution in a very complex manner.
claims.source: The empirical data that we used to inform our simulations did also not provide explicit information about potential compensatory mutations, which arguably can influence the dynamics of resistance evolution (Andersson and Hughes, 2010) – although likely in a very complex manner, as recent studies suggest (Dunai et al., 2019).

results.result: Antimicrobial resistance threatens the efficacy of drug treatments against pathogen infections.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C7 are well-established facts in the field of antimicrobial resistance, drawing from scientific consensus and general knowledge. These are background statements that set the context for the study.

results.result: Most population genetic models consider single-step resistance, but two fundamentally different patterns exist (single-step and multi-step), and no systematic review has been conducted.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C11, C12, and C22 establish the gap in the literature that this study addresses. The claims are supported by citations and the authors' literature review (Table 1), which provides the first systematic compilation of these patterns.

results.result: A systematic literature review reveals that drug resistance evolution follows two patterns: single mutations with large benefits or multiple mutations with small benefits. Many resistance mutation benefits are below clinical MIC breakpoints, fitness costs range from 0-25% growth reduction, and AMPs show lower average benefits than ABs.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C21, C23-C28 are supported by the comprehensive literature review presented in Table 1 and Figure 1. The data compilation from multiple experimental studies provides strong evidence for the existence of both resistance patterns and the distribution of costs and benefits. The statistical analysis (R²=0.07, p=0.09) shows a very weak correlation between costs and benefits.

results.result: Resistance evolution is substantially limited if more than two mutations are required, with treatment failure probability approaching zero when three mutations are necessary.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C29-C32 are strongly supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2A. The finding is robust to variations in cost-benefit correlations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and represents a key quantitative result of the modeling study.

results.result: The extent of resistance limitation depends on drug type and pharmacokinetic profile. Constant PKs lower treatment failure most, while AMPs show increased sensitivity to PK shape, particularly with ramp PKs leading to drastically increased treatment failure in multi-step scenarios.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C39-C41, C47-C53 are supported by comprehensive simulation results across different PK profiles (Figure 3 and supplements). The paradoxical finding that AMPs perform worse with ramp PKs is explained mechanistically through selection coefficient analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B), showing that narrow MSWs can create optimal sequential selection conditions.

results.result: Higher mutational diversity was observed with single-step than multi-step resistance evolution, explained by extinction at high doses/low benefits and high mutational costs at low doses/high benefits. Diversity arises from a complex combination of selection pressure, bacterial growth, and fitness costs.
results.evaluation: Claims C34, C36-C37, C78, C82 are supported by simulation results (Figure 2B) and mechanistic explanations. The counterintuitive finding is well-explained through analytical results showing invasion conditions (C35) and is consistent with experimental observations (C38). The non-trivial relationship between diversity and treatment failure is demonstrated across multiple conditions.

results.result: With multi-step resistance, adaptive treatment delays treatment failure longer than aggressive treatment, with a much lower threshold for when adaptive treatment becomes favorable compared to single-step resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C60-C63 are supported by analytical derivations and simulation results (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The mechanistic explanation that only the subpopulation one mutation away constitutes the risk population (C61) provides clear theoretical justification for the lower threshold in multi-step scenarios.

results.result: AMP treatments show lower treatment failure and mutational diversity than AB treatments with peak and constant PKs, with mutations accumulating at sublethal doses but maximal diversity substantially lower for AMPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 are supported by simulation results (Figures 2 and 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) using empirically-derived PD parameters. The findings are consistent with prior work (C18, C19) and empirical studies (C45 cites Andersson and Hughes, 2014).

results.result: HGT carriers dominated the pathogen population at treatment end, but HGT addition did not change treatment failure probability. Initial population rescue is due to mutations, with HGT resistance acquired later, and this only occurs if initial HGT acquisition rate exceeds mutation rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66, C103 are supported by simulation results (Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 4). The finding that HGT doesn't change treatment failure probability is conditional on acquisition rates being lower than mutation rates, which is explicitly stated and justified with calculations (C104).

results.result: Bacteriostatic antimicrobials slow mutation rise only for ramp and constant PK treatments, not peak PKs. Peak PKs allow bacterial regrowth due to drug decay, increasing treatment failure, especially with multi-step resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 are supported by simulation results (Figure 3—figure supplement 6). The mechanistic explanation for why peak PKs behave differently is provided (C55), though this is based on model inference rather than direct experimental validation.

results.result: Multi-step resistance is a surprisingly strong inhibitor of resistance evolution and mutational diversity, with the number of mutations necessary strongly affecting treatment outcome predictions in a manner robust to variations in mutation rates and costs.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 are supported by comprehensive simulation results and robustness analyses (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 5, Figure 3). The finding is described as 'surprisingly strong' and is robust across different parameter assumptions.

results.result: Experimental support shows that limited mutational input to low benefits decreases resistance evolution. The magnitude of resistance benefit correlates with mechanism: efflux pumps yield low benefits while specific target mutations yield high benefits. MIC increase is low for drugs with unspecific resistance mechanisms and high for specific target modifications.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C77 are supported by multiple citations to experimental and review studies. These claims provide mechanistic context linking the observed patterns to molecular mechanisms of resistance, though the authors note that specific mutations are generally not known in their compiled data (Table 1).

results.result: The parameter κ (steepness of dose-response curve) governs not only MSW size but qualitatively shapes selection pressure for resistance evolution.
results.evaluation: Claim C85 is supported by selection coefficient analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 5C) showing that κ and ψ_min independently shape selection pressure in qualitatively and quantitatively different ways. This provides mechanistic insight into why AMPs behave differently than ABs.

results.result: Natural AMP expression patterns resemble ramp PKs, suggesting AMP cocktails may be favorable to limit resistance evolution. Multi-step patterns are common for AMP resistance while both patterns are common for ABs. Clinical AMPs like colistin and daptomycin are applied as short IV treatments (peak PKs) and remain active as last-resort drugs.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C94 connect simulation findings to natural systems and clinical practice through citations. The speculation about AMP cocktails (C89) is appropriately qualified as a suggestion. The claims about clinical practice (C91-C92) and resistance patterns (C93-C94) are well-supported by citations.

results.result: Distributions of mutational effects are rarely characterized experimentally but are crucial for PKPD models. Benefits and costs likely vary between mutations, and epistasis can affect evolutionary pathways, though main results are expected to be robust to epistatic effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C99 identify limitations and discuss model assumptions. C95-C96 are supported by citations and the authors' simulation results. C97 is an inference from Figure 1B data. C98 is supported by citation. C99 is a speculation about robustness that is reasonable but not directly tested.

results.result: Compensatory mutations can influence resistance evolution dynamics in complex ways and might be necessary for multi-step resistance patterns to arise by increasing selection coefficients of early mutational subpopulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C102 are speculative inferences about compensatory mutations. C100 is supported by citations, but C101-C102 are speculations based on simulation results without direct testing. The authors acknowledge that their data did not provide explicit information about compensatory mutations.

results.result: Using typical conjugation rates, environmental HGT donors must exceed 10^5 cells/ml to be faster than chromosomal mutations. Plasmid transfer rates are variable, increased at low AB doses, biased toward clone-mates, but show no correlation with genetic distance. For AMPs, HGT spread from gut microbiota is low, so treatment failure risk is mainly shaped by beneficial mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C110 are supported by calculations based on cited experimental values and citations to relevant studies. C104 provides a quantitative threshold calculation. C109-C110 specifically address AMPs and are supported by citation (Kintses et al., 2019) and inference from simulation results.

results.result: Fast growth and high mutation rates can lead to significant heterogeneity in bacterial populations, which would increase treatment failure by giving a 'head-start' in mutation accumulation. Starting from heterogeneous populations results in less than 50% treatment failure on average in multi-step scenarios.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C113 address the effect of pre-existing heterogeneity. C111 is general knowledge, C112 is a logical inference, and C113 is supported by simulation results (Figure 2—figure supplement 6, Figure 3—figure supplement 7). The finding that multi-step resistance still limits treatment failure even with heterogeneous starting populations is important.

results.result: When starting from populations with pre-existing resistance mutations, adaptive treatment can be more effective than aggressive treatment. In drug-free environments, lower resistant cell frequency is expected for multi-step patterns. Adaptive treatment is likely superior for drugs where multi-step patterns are most common.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C116 are inferences from the adaptive treatment analysis (Figure 4) and the prevalence of multi-step patterns. C114 is an inference from the threshold analysis, C115 is a logical inference about probability, and C116 synthesizes multiple findings. These are reasonable conclusions but represent extensions beyond directly tested scenarios.

results.result: The model assumptions are not specific to bacterial populations or antimicrobials, making them broadly applicable to other drug treatments like cancer therapy.
results.evaluation: Claim C117 is a reasonable inference about model generalizability supported by citation to cancer therapy modeling (Chakrabarti and Michor, 2017). The claim is appropriately qualified and represents a discussion point rather than a tested result.

results.result: Treatment strategies should be guided by understanding resistance evolution, a task facilitated by mathematical modeling. PKPD models describe drug concentration changes and effects on pathogen populations. The availability of single-step or multi-step resistance patterns affects evolutionary dynamics in response to treatment strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10, C13 provide background and motivation for the study. C8-C9 are supported by citations to prior work. C10 is a standard definition. C13 is a logical inference that is supported by the simulation results throughout the paper.

results.result: Long-lasting infections like P. aeruginosa and TB evolve resistance via de novo mutations within the host during treatment. HGT is common in hospital-acquired infections and shorter treatment durations.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16 provide context for focusing on de novo mutations and are supported by citations to relevant studies (Oliver et al., 2000; Castro et al., 2020; Dortet et al., 2018). These are background claims that justify the study's focus.

results.result: AMPs are key innate defense components and new antimicrobial drugs that work by disrupting bacterial membranes. They significantly reduce resistance evolution risk compared to conventional ABs, partly due to higher killing rates. Recent studies have questioned radical pathogen elimination strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C20 provide background on AMPs and adaptive treatment strategies, all supported by citations to relevant literature. These establish the rationale for comparing AMPs to ABs and for investigating adaptive treatment strategies.

results.result: Higher genetic diversity increases survival probability and adaptive potential. A mutant can invade if its death rate is lower than the sensitive strain's. Resistance alleles with low costs are favored. Treatment failure and diversity are connected non-trivially. Adaptive treatment maintains sensitive populations for competitive inhibition while managing mutational risk, with a threshold for when it becomes more effective than aggressive treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C33, C35, C38, C42, C57-C59 provide theoretical background and mechanistic explanations. C33 and C38 are supported by citations. C35 is an analytical result from the model. C42 is an inference from simulation results. C57-C59 define and explain adaptive treatment, with C59 supported by citation to Hansen et al., 2017.

results.result: Mutational diversity can increase adaptation by fixing mildly deleterious mutations that act as stepping stones for multi-drug resistance. Diversity during treatment helps determine if dose escalation would be beneficial. The number of resistance mutations emerging can estimate MSW width. Drug choice should depend on both PD characteristics and specific PK in the target body compartment.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81, C83 discuss implications of diversity findings. C79 is supported by citation (Van Egeren et al., 2018). C80 is a logical inference about clinical implications. C81 is an inference supported by simulation results (Figure 3—figure supplement 3). C83 is a key conclusion from the complex PK-PD interactions observed.

results.result: Bacteriostatic effects can lead to different trends for PK and PD influence, making peak PKs the least favorable drug administration route.
results.evaluation: Claim C84 is supported by simulation results (Figure 3—figure supplement 6). This finding contrasts with bactericidal drug results and highlights the importance of drug action mechanism in determining optimal administration routes.
